newsitem.title: UK: France alone on Zaire, others see Mobutu power over.
newsitem.headline: France alone on Zaire, others see Mobutu power over.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Western powers think rebels in Zaire have definitively broken the power of President Mobutu Sese Seko and, with the exception of France, see no role for an international force there until the conflict is over.

Diplomats say French appeals for humanitarian intervention are unlikely to move the United States, Britain and others from a belief that sending troops now to the vast central African state would be risky and pointless.

French President Jacques Chirac denounced what he called a "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire and appealed to the international community on Tuesday to force a ceasefire there and take emergency humanitarian action.
But diplomats say there is little appetite for putting troops at risk when it is clear that the rebels are not prepared to negotiate while they are making major advances.

Under the leadership of Laurent Kabila, the rebels' stated aim is to depose the autocratic Mobutu, who has ruled Zaire for more than a quarter of a century and is widely blamed for plunging the country into poverty and disarray.

"It seems clear to most of us that Mobutu's power is broken and that the country is increasingly fragmented," said one Western diplomat. "There is no chance of troops going in until there is a ceasefire or until it's over. No one puts their troops at that kind of risk."
During the Cold War, Western powers backed Mobutu as a force for stability and a bulwark against the spread of communism, helping to keep him in power.

While this is no longer the case, Paris wants to prevent the breakup of Zaire and has backed the ailing Mobutu, now convalescing on the French Riviera after prostate cancer surgery, as the best guarantor of stability.
France has also suggested its allies have turned a blind eye to the support from Uganda and other neighbouring countries for the rebels.
But Washington and others are concerned that forcing a ceasefire would give support to Mobutu's shaky position, at a time when they have no wish to prop him up any longer.
The United States, Britain and former colonial power Belgium no longer have the strategic or economic interests that they once protected in Africa's third-largest country.

They also want to avoid any repeat of last year's embarrassment, when Western countries spent weeks planning a force to help Rwandan refugees in eastern Zaire, only to abandon the idea when many of them decided to go home.

Paris backs a proposal from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for an international humanitarian intervention force, which the United States has rejected. Without Washington's backing, intervention of any kind in Zaire is highly unlikely.
Another diplomat said: "The consequences of Zaire breaking up may be terrible. But it is happening and we cannot wish it were not so."
The rebels have captured a swathe of eastern Zaire, driving Rwandan Hutu refugees before them, and now threaten the government stronghold of Kisangani. They announced other advances on Tuesday.

Kabila has accepted a five-point peace plan, put forward last month by the U.N. Security Council and backed by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), as a basis for negotiation but rejected its call for a ceasefire.
South Africa has played a leading role in trying to broker an end to the fighting, with little success so far.

Recent reports of alleged massacres of Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire, at the heart of French concerns, have been denied by the rebels. The U.N. refugee agency says that some 400,000 refugees remain unaccounted for in Zaire.
The European Union's humanitarian affairs commissioner, Emma Bonino, said on Monday that rebels were hunting them down "like wild game."
A vocal critic of Western governments, Bonino accused the international community of "cowardice, a lot of lies and an enormous dose of cynicism".
